paragraphs: One-line judgment: Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants are not about "standing at the fuel dispenser and flicking a switch" but about linking fuel and fluid supply, tire and accessory replacement, cashiering and sales, and site cleaning and documentation into a checkable service process; people who only want to work with their hands and are unwilling to verify fluid specifications, nozzles, receipts, and safety procedures are not suited to it.

Signals to keep exploring: you can verify the fuel type, fluid specifications, and capacities against the vehicle or boat manual, are willing to wear protective equipment outdoors in all-weather conditions and handle spills per the rules, can keep cashiering and records accurate during queues and rushed orders, and stop and ask for guidance when the fuel type, fluid specifications, or safety conditions are unclear.

Conditions for pausing your investment: you have not yet completed one full workflow of fueling, fluid checks, tire or accessory replacement, and cashiering records under any supervised conditions, or you can only describe your interest as "liking cars and boats"; also do not treat course grades, one time helping a friend change a tire, or being able to drive as proof that you can operate fueling equipment independently, handle hazardous chemicals, or handle spills. Work involving fuel and hazardous chemicals must be carried out by organizations and personnel with the appropriate training and authorization following procedures; this page does not provide field work instructions.

Education and authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists 53-6031.00 as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0), and among respondents 59% think a high school diploma or equivalent is needed, 23% think a postsecondary certificate is needed, and 16% think less than a high school diploma is needed; on the mainland China side, fuel (gasoline and diesel) is a hazardous chemical, and the Regulations on the Safety Administration of Hazardous Chemicals require operating enterprises to obtain a hazardous chemicals business license and employees to receive safety education and training and pass assessment before taking up the job, with positions that have qualification requirements staffed by personnel who have lawfully obtained the corresponding qualifications. Courses and training, an employer's internal authorization to work, a hazardous chemicals business license, and position authorization are different statuses and must be verified item by item according to employer, position, and location.

One line: this is an occupation that turns vehicle and boat fuel, fluid, and accessory service into a checkable process; the core is supply, inspection, replacement, cashiering, and site and record management, with responsibility for fluid specifications, receipt accuracy, and work safety, rather than an interest in cars and boats or driving experience.

The work of Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants falls into three categories: fuel and routine maintenance service (adding gasoline or diesel to automobiles, buses, trucks, boats, and other vehicles; checking tire pressure and the levels of fuel, engine oil, transmission fluid, coolant, and battery fluid and topping them up as needed; greasing and lubricating specified parts; and performing minor repairs such as oil changes, filter changes, brake adjustments, and spark plug replacement); sales and cashiering (selling and installing accessories such as batteries, wiper blades, fan belts, light bulbs, and headlights, accepting cash or swiping the customer's credit card, making change and issuing receipts, and compiling daily reports on fuel, oil, and accessory sales); and site and records (cleaning the parking area, office, restrooms, and equipment and hauling away trash, ordering stock and pricing and shelving it, maintaining customer records and periodically reminding them of due services, and providing customers with local road condition information). All three categories presuppose stopping and escalating when the fuel type, fluid specifications, or safety conditions are unclear.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 53-6031.00 Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants (page updated in 2026). The official duties are to service automobiles, buses, trucks, boats, and other automotive or marine vehicles with fuel, lubricants, and accessories and collect payment for services and supplies; they may lubricate vehicles, change motor oil, refill antifreeze, or replace accessories such as wiper blades, fan belts, light bulbs, and headlights, and may repair or replace tires; there are 14 official tasks, covering accepting cash and card payments and issuing receipts; checking tire pressure and the levels of fuel and of fluids such as engine oil, transmission fluid, coolant, and battery fluid and topping them up as needed; performing minor repairs such as adjusting brakes and replacing spark plugs and oil filters; cleaning the parking area and equipment and hauling away trash; ordering stock and pricing and shelving it; selling and installing accessories; lubricating specified parts; tire rotation, testing, and repair or replacement; compiling daily sales reports; cleaning windshields; starting fuel pumps and filling to the specified level; testing and charging batteries; maintaining customer records and periodically reminding them of due services; and providing customers with local road condition information. Field boundaries: the summary page does not publish importance scores for tasks, and the task list describes the work of the group as a whole and does not mean every job performs all tasks. The details do in fact show Importance: cashiering 91, tire pressure and fluids 81, minor repair 80; 8 are Core and 6 are Supplemental (daily reports 81, windshields 80, fueling 74, batteries 70, customer records 68, road conditions 34). The scores are not frequency or authorization for all positions.

Inspection and minor repair | According to the actual task scope | Officially this includes adjusting brakes, replacing spark plugs and oil filters, and tire repair and replacement; the specific tool procedures and personnel conditions should be verified separately, and whole-system repair ability is not inferred from the occupation name.

Sales and cashiering | Make the accounts checkable | Take the part by model and install the accessory, price it, collect payment, make change and issue a receipt, compile the daily fuel, oil, and accessory sales report, and reconcile cash and receipts at shift handover.

Article 94 provides that when personal safety is directly endangered, the shift leader, team leader, or dispatcher may immediately issue an order to stop production and evacuate while ensuring safety; this does not authorize ordinary attendants to handle matters beyond their authority, nor does it require personnel to wait for ordinary permits before avoiding danger. Complete site recovery procedures were not obtained this round. Rules applicable to waste must be verified separately, and complete on-site procedures were not obtained.
Site and inventory | Keep the site usable | Clean the parking area, office area, and sanitary facilities and haul away trash, order stock, price and shelve it, and maintain inventory records.

Records and customer follow-up | Make the process reviewable | Maintain customer records and periodically remind customers of due services, provide local road condition and safety information, and report disputes per institutional procedures.

Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants handle fuel supply, routine fluid and tire service, and cashiering and site maintenance, and are responsible for fluid specifications, receipt accuracy, and work safety; automotive service technicians and mechanics focus on fault diagnosis and repair; bus and truck mechanics and diesel engine specialists focus on heavy vehicle and engine repair; tire repairers and changers focus on tire mounting, demounting, and repair; vehicle and equipment cleaners focus on washing and cleaning; aircraft service attendants focus on fueling and servicing aircraft; home appliance repairers focus on household appliance repair. Reviewable service and cashiering records

The type and quantity of fuel or fluid added, the items checked and replaced, the accessory model and quantity, the payment method and amount, how spills or anomalies were handled, and the inventory and cash statement at shift handover.
The individual and the station manager or shift supervisor

The accuracy of fueling, inspection, replacement, and cashiering records is the individual's responsibility; authority to handle fuel and hazardous chemicals operations, spill response, and equipment faults is granted by organizations and personnel with the appropriate training and authorization following procedures, and when conditions are unclear work must stop and be escalated.
Education and preparation

O*NET lists 53-6031.00 as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0), typically requiring a high school diploma or equivalent (some positions require less), with on-the-job training ranging from a few days to a year; among the education levels published on the page, 59% is requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, 23% is requiring a postsecondary certificate, and 16% is requiring less than a high school diploma; O*NET also lists 2 national certifications and training program entry points. On the mainland China side, training is mainly for positions such as gas station and marina service, automotive operation and maintenance, and transportation operation service, with specific requirements set by the employer.
Not interchangeable

Education, on-the-job training, institutional authorization to work, a hazardous chemicals business license and position authorization, and lubrication certifications (such as Machinery Lubrication Technician Level I and Certified Lubrication Specialist) are different statuses: education does not bring a business license, and certification does not mean you can add fuel or handle spills in any setting.

Occupational definition

The U.S. side is O*NET 53-6031.00 (Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants); on the mainland China side you must first identify whether the position belongs to a gas station or gas-fueling station, an auto service and quick-repair shop, marina and yacht club fuel supply, parking and fleet service, or hotel and property vehicle service, because different employers differ greatly in their requirements for hazardous chemicals, fire safety, and handling customer money.
Education and major pathways

On the U.S. side O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0), typically requiring a high school diploma or equivalent and providing from a few days to a year of on-the-job training; on the mainland China side, training is mainly for positions such as gas station and marina service, automotive operation and maintenance, and transportation operation service, with specific requirements set by the employer.
Authorization to work and work permits

On the mainland China side, gasoline, diesel, and the like are hazardous chemicals, and units operating gasoline or diesel must obtain a hazardous chemicals business license under the Regulations on the Safety Administration of Hazardous Chemicals (promulgated by State Council Order No. 591 and revised in 2013), and employees must receive safety education and position technical training and pass assessment before taking up the job, with positions that have qualification requirements staffed by personnel who have lawfully obtained the corresponding qualifications; on the U.S. side it is determined by employer procedures and job authorization. Before starting, verify pre-job training, work permits, and review processes; this cannot be inferred directly from education or certification.
Equipment and site safety

Fuel and fluid handling must meet the applicable hazardous chemicals and fire safety requirements (on the mainland China side, see the provisions of the Regulations on the Safety Administration of Hazardous Chemicals on business licensing, employee training, and storage management); nozzles, air compressors, and lifting equipment must be used according to the manual and institutional procedures, and spills must be handled per the emergency response process. This page does not constitute field work instructions.
Shifts and outdoor work

Common arrangements include rotating morning, afternoon, and night shifts and holiday shifts, outdoor all-weather work, and continuous cashiering and service during customer peak hours; when comparing jobs, put the shift structure, outdoor work hours, overtime and compensatory rest, and whether marina or night work is involved into the written terms.
Continuing training and review

Equipment and systems update quickly (O*NET lists 7 software skills, 6 of which are marked as hot technologies, with browser types appearing in about 33% of job requirements), requiring ongoing continuing training and peer review; before starting, confirm the training arrangements, the frequency of spill and emergency drills, and how skill updates are supported.

entries.answer: There are three core categories of tasks: adding gasoline or diesel to automobiles, buses, trucks, boats, and the like; checking tire pressure and the levels of fuel, engine oil, transmission fluid, coolant, and battery fluid and topping them up as needed; and performing minor repairs such as oil changes, filter changes, and brake adjustments; selling and installing accessories such as batteries, wiper blades, fan belts, and light bulbs, accepting cash or swiping a card, making change and issuing receipts, and compiling daily sales reports; and cleaning the parking area, office area, and equipment and hauling away trash, ordering stock and pricing and shelving it, and maintaining customer records and periodically reminding customers of due services. The U.S. side corresponds to O*NET 53-6031.00, whose official duties are to supply vehicles with fuel, lubricants, and accessories and collect payment, and they may lubricate vehicles, change motor oil, refill antifreeze, or replace accessories, and may repair or replace tires.

Article 54 requires professional training and assessment for employees of operating enterprises, and the principal responsible person and safety management personnel must additionally be assessed by the emergency management department. Article 91 of that law covers unit emergency plans, rescue arrangements, and drills; Article 93 requires the principal responsible person to organize rescue and reporting immediately per the plan when an accident occurs. Article 94 provides that when personal safety is directly endangered, the shift leader, team leader, or dispatcher may immediately issue an order to stop production and evacuate while ensuring safety; this does not authorize ordinary attendants to handle matters beyond their authority, nor does it require personnel to wait for ordinary permits before avoiding danger. subject.summary: Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants add fuel and fluids to vehicles such as automobiles, buses, trucks, and boats, check and replace tires and accessories, collect payment, and maintain the site and inventory records, and the core is verifying against specifications, servicing by checklist, and recording accurately. The U.S. side corresponds to O*NET 53-6031.00 (Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants), in Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0), and the 2024—2034 employment projection is a decline (-1% or lower); mainland China statistics are aggregated by industry category and do not list this occupation separately, gasoline and diesel are hazardous chemicals, and the training requirements for operators and employees are set out in the Regulations on the Safety Administration of Hazardous Chemicals; industry figures do not cover night-shift and holiday allowances or sales commissions.
